messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Carpenter
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Darius Green had been working as a carpenter for years, the kind of man who was used to measuring twice, lifting carefully, and moving through a job site with practiced ease. At thirty, married and trying to keep up with the steady rhythm of work and home, he had not expected an ordinary day on a construction project to split his life into before and after. The trauma he described happened when he was on site and witnessed a serious accident involving another worker. In the seconds that followed, Darius saw the other man’s injuries at close range, with the kind of exposed, vivid detail that still came back to him without warning. He remembered blood on skin, the shock in people’s faces, and the sudden, overwhelming sense that the scene had become real in a way he could not get out of his body. Even now, he struggled to put the event into words. When he tried to explain it in session, he would stop, stare down, and say only that it was “bad” and “all over the place,” as if language failed him before the memory did.

In the months after that day, Darius began to notice that certain moments could throw him straight back into the scene. Sometimes it happened so abruptly that it seemed to arrive before he had time to think: a smell in the air, a glimpse of a wound on someone else, or, most unsettling of all, an unexpected touch on his arm or shoulder. Physical contact that would normally have meant nothing could jolt him into a full-body reaction, with his chest tightening and his attention narrowing as if the accident were unfolding again in front of him. He described those episodes as though the room changed around him, and he was no longer in his kitchen or on a job site but back at the moment of the injury, seeing everything at once. The memory did not come to him as a simple picture. It returned with its full sensory force, so that he could almost taste one particular taste associated with the event, the one that had become tied to the aftermath on the site, and he would feel nauseated by how immediate and complete it was. He said the worst part was that it could happen “out of nowhere,” with nothing obvious to prepare him, and then he was back there before he had the chance to brace himself.

As time went on, Darius found himself avoiding any thought of the event because even a brief attempt to go over it made him feel flooded and cornered. He developed habits he recognized as desperate attempts to get away from what was happening inside him. When the memories surged, he would deliberately try to leave his body or blank out, focusing on that thin edge of distance rather than on what he felt. At other times, especially in the evenings, he would eat excessively in the hope that being physically overfull would drown out the distress. These efforts brought short-lived relief, but they left him ashamed and increasingly convinced that he could not trust himself to stay steady when something reminded him of what he had seen. He began saying that he was “not the same guy” and that the trauma had permanently changed him for the worse. That belief hardened over time into a bleak certainty that his life had been destroyed by what happened, not in a dramatic public way, but in the quieter sense that he no longer felt like the man who used to work with confidence, come home tired, and be present with his wife without constantly checking his own reactions.

At work, the consequences became harder to hide. As a carpenter, Darius could not avoid the sight of cuts, scrapes, or more serious injuries when the job was rough, and those visible wounds could seize his attention before he had a chance to look away. He found himself uneasy when coworkers put a hand on his back to get his attention or when someone reached for a tool near him. He started to keep more distance, and over weeks that distance began to affect how he functioned on the crew. At home, his wife noticed that he was withdrawn after work and preoccupied with not thinking about the accident, as though silence itself might protect him from another sudden return of the memory. He had come to believe that if he let his mind go near it, he would lose control, collapse under the weight of what he had seen, or discover that some permanent damage had already been done.

By the time Darius sought help, he was exhausted by the effort of managing the memories, the fear of triggers, and the shame he felt about his own reactions. What brought him in was not a single crisis but the accumulation of them: the repeated shock of being pulled back into the scene, the way his attempts to shut it down were no longer enough, and the growing fear that he would keep living as if part of him were still trapped on that job site. He said he wanted to understand why the memory could still hit him so hard and so suddenly, and whether there was any way to feel like himself again. More than anything, he was afraid that the damage was permanent, but he was also hoping that therapy might help him find a way to stay present in his own life without being ambushed by what he had witnessed.
